Normal Antenatal Renal US

Hydronephrosis

Notes

Definitions

CORE TERMS

Hydronephrosis = dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces (the collecting system). It describes anatomy, not cause — a dilated system is not necessarily obstructed.
Antenatal hydronephrosis (ANH) = hydronephrosis first detected on prenatal (fetal) ultrasound.
Commonly used thresholds: renal pelvis AP diameter ≥ 4 mm at 16–27 wk or ≥ 7 mm at ≥ 28 wk; ≥ 10 mm postnatally.

EXTRA

RULE OF THUMB

Dilated ≠ obstructed. Many ANH cases are physiologic or transient — the postnatal work-up exists to find the kidneys that are actually at risk (obstruction, reflux, bladder outlet obstruction).

Normal antenatal renal US — collecting system not distended.

Hydronephrosis — large anechoic (black) dilated pelvis with dilated calyces.

ABBREVIATIONS USED IN THIS GUIDE

ANH antenatal hydronephrosis · AF amniotic fluid UPJ(O) ureteropelvic junction (obstruction)

UVJ ureterovesical junction · VUR vesicoureteral reflux PUV posterior urethral valves · UDT undescended testis

VCUG voiding cystourethrogram · IVP intravenous pyelogram MCDK multicystic dysplastic kidney · PCKD polycystic kidney disease

T½ washout half-time on diuretic renal scan

EEC exstrophy–epispadias complex · TOF tetralogy of Fallot

  • Voiding ( 1st void, straining, wetting the diaper)

Oligohydramnios

  • OLIGOHYDRAMNIOS = amniotic fluid <500cc (pocket <2cm)
  • Before 16-18 wks, most of AF is a placental transudate
  • By 20-22 wks, most of AF is fetal urine
  • Urine production starts at ~12 wks
  • Oligohydramnios that develops only after 18-20 weeks likely represents GU tract obstruction or abnormal renal development.

Oligohydramnios that appears only after 18–20 wk → GU obstruction or abnormal kidneys

DANGER POINT

Before 16–18 wk most AF is a placental transudate, so early AF volume says little about the kidneys. Once the kidneys make most of the fluid (20–22 wk), oligohydramnios developing only after 18–20 wk most likely means GU tract obstruction or abnormal renal development.

CLINICAL LINK

Low AF in mid-gestation restricts fetal lung growth → pulmonary hypoplasia. That is why a baby with PUV may need NICU respiratory support before anything urological is done.

TestWhat it showsUse it to…

Notes

Diuretic renogram (Lasix renal scan)

HOW TO READ IT

Pre-Lasix phase: both kidneys take up tracer (gives split function); tracer collects in the pelvis.
Lasix given (here ~20–27 min) → diuresis should wash tracer out into the bladder.
T½ = time for half the tracer to leave the kidney after Lasix. Short T½ = drains well; a curve that stays flat = obstruction.

Pre-Lasix — tracer accumulates in both kidneys; bladder fills.

Post-Lasix — tracer clears from both kidneys into the bladder.

No UPJ obstruction — both curves fall promptly after Lasix. T½: R = 6 min, L = 2 min.

NUMBERS TO KNOW

T½ < 10 min = normal drainage · 10–20 min = indeterminate · > 20 min = obstructed. Split function < 40% in the affected kidney is significant.

Notes

Postnatal work-up checklist

1

2

3

Serum creatinine — when and why?

Gives baseline renal function (essential in bilateral hydro, PUV, solitary kidney). Draw it after ~48 h: in the first days it reflects the motherʼs creatinine.

Prophylactic antibiotic

Protects a dilated, possibly refluxing or obstructed system from UTI while the work-up is pending.

Repeat US ± VCUG or nuclear scan

US confirms and grades the dilatation; VCUG if reflux or PUV is suspected; nuclear scan if obstruction is suspected. Routine first US is usually done after 48 h (neonatal oliguria can hide dilatation) — earlier if bilateral hydro or PUV is suspected.

EXTRA

Added explanationThe routine first postnatal US is usually done after 48 h (neonatal oliguria can hide dilatation) — earlier if bilateral hydro or PUV is suspected.

RULES OF THUMB

Unilateral → UPJO is the single most common cause.
Bilateral in a boy → exclude PUV first (it is the dangerous one). Bilateral in a girl → PUV is off the list; think VUR.
VUR appears in both columns — it is a cause of ~a third of unilateral ANH and a key bilateral cause.

Case 1 · Bilateral Hydronephrosis in a Boy

Posterior urethral valves

CASE 1
2-day-old term boy (SVD) — bilateral hydronephrosis on antenatal US
What are the possible causes? How would you manage him?

DEFINITION

Posterior urethral valve (PUV) = a congenital obstructive membrane in the posterior urethra that impedes antegrade flow of urine. Back-pressure dilates everything above it: posterior urethra → bladder (thick, trabeculated) → ureters → kidneys.

  • Newborn boy, bilateral ANH, thick bladder and dilated posterior urethra → best study micturating cystourethrogram (VCUG). 437 ×3
Notes

Imaging & endoscopy

Postnatal US — hydronephrotic kidneys with dilated calyces and a distended bladder.

Fetal US — distended bladder funnelling into a dilated posterior urethra (“keyholeˮ sign).

VCUG — large irregular bladder above a dilated posterior urethra

(left); reflux into a dilated, tortuous ureter and collecting system (right).

Oblique voiding views (L, R) — markedly dilated posterior urethra ending abruptly at the valves.

Cystoscopy — the obstructing valve membrane seen in the posterior urethra.

Initial Management

1) 1ST step of management : Bladder drainage (permits medical stabilization)

2) Effective NICU support for issues with pulmonary hypoplasia & renal insufficiency.

3) Lab investigations

  • Electrolyte, creatinine, BUN: may take 48hrs to be accurate.

4) Prophylactic Abx.

5) Cystoscopy and Valve ablation. (Definitive treatment)

Notes

Initial management

1

2

3

4

5

Bladder drainage — the FIRST step

Decompresses the obstructed system and permits medical stabilization.

Effective NICU support

For pulmonary hypoplasia and renal insufficiency.

Lab investigations

Electrolytes, creatinine, BUN — may take 48 h to be accurate (early values reflect the mother).

Prophylactic antibiotics

Dilated, refluxing, obstructed system = high UTI risk.

Cystoscopy and valve ablation — DEFINITIVE treatment

Once the baby is stable.

HIGH-RISK PATTERN

Boy + bilateral hydroureteronephrosis + distended thick-walled bladder + dilated posterior urethra (± oligohydramnios) = PUV until proven otherwise. The threats to life are pulmonary hypoplasia and renal insufficiency.

REMEMBER THE ORDER

Drain first, ablate later. The catheter buys time to stabilize the babyʼs lungs, fluids and electrolytes and to get a true creatinine before definitive valve ablation.

  • Newborn boy, bilateral hydronephrosis, bladder wall hypertrophy, catheter already inserted → best treatment PUV ablation. 437

Case 2 · Unilateral Hydronephrosis

Ureteropelvic junction obstruction

CASE 2
5-day-old boy — unilateral hydronephrosis diagnosed on antenatal US
What are the possible causes? How would you approach him?

UPJ OBSTRUCTION — KEY FACTS

Most common cause of UNILATERAL hydronephrosis in the fetal kidney (39–64% of unilateral ANH).
M > F
L > R
Hydronephrosis without hydroureter — the ureter below the narrowing is normal calibre.

WORK-UP & MANAGEMENT

No need for urgent intervention unless the baby develops pyelonephritis → drain with a nephrostomy tube or stent.
Repeat US and a diuretic renal scan to judge drainage and function.
Treatment is surgical: pyeloplasty.

UPJO — dilated renal pelvis and calyces above a narrowed UPJ; normal ureter below.

  • Most common cause of antenatal hydronephrosis → pelviureteric junction obstruction. 439

Imaging in Case 2

US — RT kidney: marked hydronephrosis (dilated pelvis and calyces); LT kidney: normal; bladder (right) normal.

Pre-Lasix — tracer pools in the dilated right collecting system.

Post-Lasix — left clears; right stays full.

RT UPJ obstruction — the left curve falls after Lasix (19 min); the right plateaus and never halves. T½ R = N/A (not reached).

Notes

Pyeloplasty

APPROACH

Open / laparoscopic / robotic.

WHEN TO OPERATE

Split function < 40% or a fall of > 10%
Worsening dilatation on serial US
Obstructed drainage on renal scan
Symptoms: pain, pyelonephritis, stones

EXTRA

Dismembered pyeloplasty — (a) narrowed UPJ excised, (b) ureter spatulated and re-anastomosed to the pelvis over a stent, (c) wide, funnel-shaped repair.

DANGER POINT

Pyelonephritis in an obstructed kidney needs drainage (nephrostomy tube or stent) — it is the one situation in UPJO where you intervene urgently.

Vesicoureteral reflux

CASE 3
5-day-old girl — bilateral hydronephrosis on antenatal US
What are the possible causes? How would you approach her?

FIRST THOUGHT

She is a girl, so PUV is excluded — the remaining bilateral causes are VUR, urethral aplasia, prune belly, megacystis–megaureter and PCKD. VUR leads the list.

Notes

Grading (I–V)

GradeContrast reaches…
IA non-dilated ureter only
IIPelvis and calyces, without dilation
IIIMild–moderate dilation of ureter, pelvis and calyces; minimal blunting of the fornices
IVModerate ureteral tortuosity and dilation of pelvis and calyces
VGross dilation of ureter, pelvis and calyces; loss of papillary impressions; ureteral tortuosity

Principles of Management

1. Spontaneous resolution is very common

2. High-grade VUR is less likely to resolve spontaneously

3. Extended use of prophylactic Abx is benign

4. Success rate with surgical correction is very high

Treatment options

OptionWhat it is
ObservationWatchful waiting with follow-up imaging — relies on spontaneous resolution.
Prophylactic antibioticsLow-dose daily antibiotic to prevent UTIs while reflux resolves.
Deflux injectionSurgical (endoscopic): a bulking agent injected under the ureteric orifice so it closes during bladder filling.
Ureteric reimplantationSurgical (open): the ureter is re-tunnelled under the bladder mucosa to create an anti- reflux valve.

Notes

Be aware

DO NOT CIRCUMCISE

The foreskin is tissue for the repair — a baby with hypospadias should not be circumcised before the urologist sees him.

CHECK THE TESTES

Hypospadias with undescended testes (especially proximal hypospadias or impalpable testes) raises concern for a disorder of sex development → needs evaluation (e.g. karyotype).

EXTRA

Surgical repair

TIMING & STAGES

Repair at 6–12 months of age, in 1 or 2 stages. One stage usually suits distal cases with mild curvature; staged repair suits proximal cases with severe curvature.

1

Hydronephrosis = dilated pelvis and calyces; dilated ≠ obstructed. ANH = found on fetal US.

2

Oligohydramnios = AF < 500 cc (pocket < 2 cm). Urine starts ~12 wk; by 20–22 wk AF is mostly fetal urine → oligohydramnios after 18–20 wk = GU obstruction / abnormal kidneys → pulmonary hypoplasia risk.

3

Tests: US = anatomy · VCUG = reflux + urethra · renal scan = function + drainage (T½). No IVP.

4

Neonatal creatinine reflects the mother — it takes ~48 h to be accurate.

5

Unilateral ANH → UPJO (39–64%); M > F, L > R; hydronephrosis without hydroureter.

6

Bilateral ANH in a boy → PUV until proven otherwise. First step = bladder drainage; definitive = cystoscopic valve ablation.

7

Bilateral ANH in a girl → PUV impossible → think VUR → VCUG.

8

Renal scan: draining kidney washes out after Lasix (e.g. T½ 2–6 min); obstructed kidney plateaus (T½ not reached).

9

UPJO: no urgent intervention unless pyelonephritis (→ nephrostomy / stent); treatment = pyeloplasty (open / lap / robotic).

10

VUR: grades I–V; resolution common but less likely in high grade; prophylactic Abx are safe; Deflux / reimplantation very successful.

11

Hypospadias: ventral meatus + ventral curve + dorsal hood; ~1 in 250; no circumcision; check for UDT; repair 6–12 mo, 1 or 2 stages.

12

EEC: epispadias (dorsal, M > F, repair > 1 yr, incontinence) → bladder exstrophy (> 50%) → cloacal exstrophy (GI involvement).

13

Prune belly triad: weak abdominal wall + bilateral UDT + dilated GU tract; associated TOF / VSD.
